Review of the textbook by W.N. Platonov:
System of athlete's preparation in Olympic sport.
General theory and prac

paration in Olympic sport.
General theory and practical implications
(Volume I)
by
Vladimir Lyakh1, Kazimierz Mikołajec2, Jerzy Sadowski3, Zbigniew Witkowski4
Dariusz Gierczuk3, Karol Gryko5
One of the most extended textbooks that
was published recently was written by Platonov,
who attempted to provide comprehensive insights
into various systems of athlete's preparation in
Olympic sports. The textbook is comprised of two
volumes. The first volume is composed of 8 parts
and 32 chapters. The prese

is composed of 8 parts
and 32 chapters. The present review is devoted to
the analysis of the material contained in the first
volume.
The fifteen-year explorations started by
Platonov in 2000 resulted in writing the study
which is of vital scientific and practical importance.
The necessity of writing this study was justified by
the authors by the following:
 significant changes in sports practice,
emergence of a number of facts that required
scientific analysis and verification, the need for
im

entific analysis and verification, the need for
implementation of new components into
sports theory and methodology, which
emerged with extensive professionalization
and commercialization of Olympic sports;
 increasing social and political importance of
sports success in the Western countries;
 active participation of the governmental
bodies, commercial st ructures, industrial
companies and scientific centres in the
development of Olympic sports;
 changes in the policy of the International
Ol

s;
 changes in the policy of the International
Olympic Committee, concerning the
programme of the Ol ympic Games through
implementation of ne w sports and women's
participation in the sports which used to be
considered as men's sports;
 significant elongation of the duration of
athletic careers ranging from 20 to 30 years in
many sports, which require a more
comprehensive approach to the problems
connected with athlete's health
(the study discusses the problems of injury
rates and diseases, ov

sses the problems of injury
rates and diseases, overreaching, overtraining
and excessive overloading to the functional
systems in the human body).
Platonov explorations have been based on
scientifically verified knowledge and information
leading to the bests sports results.

In the chapters devoted to the problems of
adaptations of muscle tissue, bone tissue,
ligamentous tissue (ensuring energy supply for
proper muscle functioning), sports injuries and

the experts from Scandinavian countries,
Germany, Italy, USA, Canada, Spain and France. In
the material concerning preparation of the athlete,
the methodology of

ing preparation of the athlete,
the methodology of structuring various
components of the training process, sports
periodization and coaching aimed to reach the
highest skill level, Platonov research was based
primarily on the studies written by experts from
the Eastern European countries, supplemented
with the most recent data derived from studies
published by Western researchers.
Of several thousand publications in recent
years devoted to the analysis of the optimal
preparation of elite athl et

alysis of the optimal
preparation of elite athl etes, Platonov chose and
analysed around 40% studies.
The substantial part of the contents of the
textbook focused on the author's finding and the
results obtained by his numerous students,
presented in 70 doctoral dissertations. Especially
interesting are the results of the studies concerning
the strategy of Olympic preparation, scientific,
methodological and orga nizational problems
connected with the training process in both
individual and team

the training process in both
individual and team sports. This concerns the
programs which were successful during the
Olympic Games in 1976-2014.
In the first part of the textbook, composed
of two chapters, Platonov discusses the history of
the development of the general theory concerning
preparation of elite athl etes (Chapter 1) and
methodology of planning and implementation of
training based on modern scientific
accomplishments (Chapter 2). Analysis of the
systems of athletes' preparation was

alysis of the
systems of athletes' preparation was started by
Platonov from preparation of athletes for the
Olympic Games in ancient Greece, moving to the
second half of the 19th century, when first attempts
to organize modern knowledge in this field of
science were made. The final portion of this
discussion contains the factors which lay
foundations for the system of contemporary
knowledge about preparation of elite athletes. The
author also presented scientific centres and the
most important p

sented scientific centres and the
most important people from various countries
with the highest contribution to this process.
According to Platonov, from the
methodological standpoint, the theory of athletes'
preparation involves various areas and sports. It
concerns a significant amount of empirical and
practical information from various sports,
collected using various scientific methods. The
structure of the theory of athletes' preparation was
presented by Platonov in Figure 1.
The central par

presented by Platonov in Figure 1.
The central part (core, paradigm) of the
theory is formed through construction of basic
concepts, regularities and principles which, at the
major stage of its development, were sufficiently
generalized and invariable. The core of the theory
is based on a large collection of information
included into the peripheral part , concerning a
number of facts, hypotheses, ideas, judgements,
exceptions and paradoxical phenomena in sports
theory and practice and other area

omena in sports
theory and practice and other areas of research
(anatomy, physiology, pedagogy, genetics, sports
methodology etc.), includ ing various scientific
fields, approaches and theories (theory of
adaptation, system approach, cybernetics, theory
of functional systems et c.). As emphasized by
Platonov, knowledge related to the peripheral part
was constantly evolving, part of new ideas was
developing and adopting an important place in the
structure of the theoretical knowledge while others

tructure of the theoretical knowledge while others
were eliminated.
Using selected examples, the author
demonstrated that "any attempts to lay separate
foundations and the related principles for the
theory are counterprodu ctive and substantially
reduce the capabilities of the theory”.
In the second chapter, Platonov also
isolated 6 functions of the general theory of
athletes' preparation (descriptive, explanatory,
systematizing, predictive, critical and
methodological) and emphasized the import

ical and

detail the contemporary system of knowledge

The experience of the recent years has
indicated that the effective preparation for major
sporting events in the year round training cycle,

15, with the number of days of competitions

Furthermore, Platonov discusses the
variants of determination of results in events

ation of results in events

The final part of Chapter 4 presents the
material concerning the role and place of
competitions within the system of preparation at
various levels of sports sk ill. Platonov listed

t
various levels of sports sk ill. Platonov listed three
approaches with respect to competitions in
contemporary sports practice. The first approach
assumes athletes' striving for frequent starts and
reaching a high level of achievement in the
competitions. The other approach adopts a low-
intensity start activity, with the substantial focus of
an athlete on preparation for the major
competitions in the competitive period. In the third
variant (approach), the numb er of competitions is
high but

of the preparation process. In such competitions,
the athlete is not expected to show a high level of

is oriented towards achievement of high
performance in the preliminaries and major
sporting events". In the conclusion, Platonov
discusses positive and negat

discusses positive and negative aspects of each

In conclusion of the first part of the review,
it should be emphasized that the reader will find
all 32 chapters of the book very interesting. The
contents represent valuab le material with great
practical implications for coaches, athletes and
research workers. The text is supported by
numerous illustrations that make the book more
attra

merous illustrations that make the book more
attractive and easier to follow.
The review of the second volume will be
presented in a later issue of the JHK.

Chapter 3
Nutrition for Marathon Running
Karsten Koehler
Abstract Marathon runners can uniquely bene ﬁt from nutritional strategies that
support their training responses and/or maximize their performance during the actual
race. Promising strategies during marathon training include the adequate provision
of dietary energy, macronutrients (carbohydrates, protein), and selected micronu-
trients (e.g., iron) to meet the increased requirements of prolonged distance running.
Nutritional and training a

onged distance running.
Nutritional and training approaches aimed at increasing fat oxidation rates or
facilitating weight loss may be associated with negative effects and should therefore
be conducted with care. During the actual marathon race, runners can bene ﬁt from
carbohydrate loading strategies that serve to maximize pre-race muscle glycogen
storage capacity. Consumption of carbohydrates, ﬂuid, and sodium can prevent
preemptive fatigue due to nutrient depletion, and caffeine supplementati

to nutrient depletion, and caffeine supplementation can
provide ergogenic effects during prolonged running. Because the responses to these
nutritional interventions can vary substantially among individuals and require ﬁne
tuning depending on factors such as performance level, environmental conditions,
designated running pace, propensity for gastrointestinal discomfort, and availability
of aid stations during the race, marathon runners are highly encouraged to familiarize
themselves with these s

encouraged to familiarize
themselves with these strategies prior to utilizing them in a competitive setting.

Nutrition is a factor of paramount importance for marathon running. Adequate
nutritional strategies can support the marathon runner in achieving their goals when
training for marathon running as well as in maximizing their performance during

Due to the high load of marathon training, runners uniquely bene ﬁt from
strategies that allow them to sustain prolonged exercise at a vigorous pace and from
interventions that maximize marathon-speci ﬁc training adaptations (Stellingwerff
2013). Nutritional strategies should be aligned with the goals, requirement

characteristics of speci ﬁc training periods and consequently may vary between
general training, race-speci ﬁc training, pre-race preparation periods, and speci ﬁc
training interventions practiced only by a few (elite) runners, such as altitude
training or heat acclimatization (Stellingwerff 2012; Burke et al. 2007).
Energy production during prolonged running is almost exclusively aerobic. The
primary energy substrates utilized during mara

dration strategies may be warranted. Hyperhydration can be achieved through
consumption of excess ﬂuid and the addition of sodium to retain ﬂuid and prevent
increased urination (Shirreffs et al. 2004). Athletes are strongly advised to refrain
from prohibited hyperhydrating substances, such as glyc

prohibited hyperhydrating substances, such as glycerol (World Anti-Doping
Agency 2015). Even though endurance performance capacity can be negatively
impacted by dehydration by as little as 2 % of body weight, it has been repeatedly
reported that faster marathon runners tend to consume less ﬂuid and attain greater
levels of dehydration when compared to slower runners (Zouhal et al. 2011).
However, it remains unclear if these ﬁndings suggest that mild dehydration is
associated with a performance b

ild dehydration is
associated with a performance bene ﬁt or that faster and better-trained runners have
a greater tolerance for dehydration. Because ﬂuid losses can vary considerable
among individuals and are strongly dependent on both individual and environ-
mental factors, athletes are advised to determine their individual ﬂuid loss, and
consequently their requirements, under race-like conditions. Exercise-associated
ﬂuid losses can easily be determined by assessing changes in body weight over

etermined by assessing changes in body weight over the
course of an exercise bout (Sawka et al. 2007).
Over-consumption of ﬂuid may result in dilutional hyponatremia, which is
associated with moderate side effects, such as confusion, weakness, and fainting
(plasma Na
+ <130 mmol/L), and severe side effects, including seizures, coma, and
death (plasma Na + <126 mmol/L). In most marathon runners, hyponatremia is
asymptomatic, but it can become severe in a small proportion of athletes (Kipps
et al.

re in a small proportion of athletes (Kipps
et al. 2011), and has been linked to several fatalities during marathon races.
Hyponatremia can be prevented by avoiding excessive ﬂuid intake and by atten-
uating sodium depletion in runners who excrete salty sweat (Montain et al. 2006),
which can be reached through sodium consumption of approximately 450 mg/h
from sports beverages or the addition of salt to water and other beverages
(Murray 2007).
3.3.4 Gastrointestinal Distress
Between 10 and 95 % o

.4 Gastrointestinal Distress
Between 10 and 95 % of marathon runners experience gastrointestinal distress
during prolonged running (Jeukendrup 2011). Most runners report only mild
symptoms, such as nausea and dizziness, but more severe complications such as
stomach and intestinal cramps, vomiting, and diarrhea, may occur in a small pro-
portion of runners and can impair marathon performance substantially (Pfeiffer
3 Nutrition for Marathon Running 59

et al. 2012). Gastrointestinal distress occurs more frequently during running when
compared to other endurance exercise modes and its incidence increases with
exercise duration (Peters et al. 1999). Dietary factors that have been linked to
gastrointestinal distress include the consumption of highly concentrated sports
drinks and particularly highly concentrated CHO and/or large amounts of CHO that
may exceed the intestinal CHO absorption capacity (Sareban et al. 2015; Pfeiffer
et al. 2009; Rehre

(Sareban et al. 2015; Pfeiffer
et al. 2009; Rehrer et al. 1992). Because the gastrointestinal CHO tolerance varies
considerably among individuals and may adapt to chronically high CHO exposure,
marathon runners are encouraged to determine their individual tolerable rate of
CHO consumption (Jeukendrup 2011). Other dietary risk factors associated with
gastrointestinal distress include the consumption of fat, ﬁber, or protein while
exercising (Peters et al. 1999). Because none of these nutrients a

rs et al. 1999). Because none of these nutrients are essential for
marathon running, athletes should be discouraged from products that contain sig-
niﬁcant amounts of fat, ﬁbers, or protein during the race. There is limited evidence
that gastrointestinal distress could be linked to insuf ﬁcient ﬂuid consumption and
dehydration during prolonged running (Stuemp ﬂe et al. 2013), so that ﬂuid con-
sumption, particularly early during the race, may reduce the risk of gastrointestinal
distress. Vitamin

uce the risk of gastrointestinal
distress. Vitamin E has been linked to the prevention of intestinal ischemia during
prolonged exercise (Buchman et al. 1999), but there is no evidence that vitamin E
supplementation could reduce gastrointestinal distress during marathon running.
3.3.5 Supplements
Despite an ever-growing market for sport supplements, compelling scienti ﬁc evi-
dence for an ergogenic effect exists for only a few substances. Caffeine, when
consumed at doses of 3 –6 mg/kg, improves a

, when
consumed at doses of 3 –6 mg/kg, improves aerobic endurance performance (Burke
2008) so that caffeine can have ergogenic effects for marathon runners. Caffeine has
a half-life of 3 –5 h and should be consumed approximately 1 h prior to the race.
Slower runners may bene ﬁt from additional caffeine consumption (1 mg/kg) after
approximately 2 h into the race. Even when caffeine is consumed at later stages
during the race, performance bene ﬁts are still likely to occur (Burke 2008). Side
effe

are still likely to occur (Burke 2008). Side
effects of caffeine exist and include insomnia, tachycardia, headache, and nausea.
The effects of caffeine on exercise performance are not altered by habituation or
withdrawal (Van Soeren and Graham 1998), and the use of caffeine is currently not
banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency ( 2015).
A novel group of supplements that may be of interest for marathon runners are
dietary sources of nitrates, which can increase metabolic ef ﬁciency during sub-

ich can increase metabolic ef ﬁciency during sub-
maximal exercise via generation of nitric oxide. As such, acute supplementation of
nitrate or consumption of nitrate-rich beetroot juice of can reduce oxygen demand
and increase running economy during prolonged exercise (Barnes and Kilding
2015). However, it remains to be determined whether these effects translated into
meaningful improvements in aerobic performance, and consequently, in marathon
performance (Table 3.3).

3.3.6 Practical Recommendations
During the marathon race, athletes typically have access to aid stations, where ﬂuid
(e.g., water and sports drinks) and food (e.g. bars, gels, and bananas) are provided.
Based on availability, preference, and needs, some athletes may consider carrying
small amounts of food and/or ﬂuid in pockets or attached to belts. Elite runners
typically have access to reserved aid stations so that they can consume customized
drinks and foods during the race without having to

rinks and foods during the race without having to carry these items.
The use of sport drinks is bene ﬁcial because they provide ﬂuid as well as CHO
and electrolytes, which both facilitate ﬂuid uptake. The CHO concentration of a
drink can be tailored such that both ﬂuid and CHO requirements are met. CHO
concentrations should be in the range of 4 –8 % (40 –80 g per L) in order to avoid
delayed gastric emptying as well as gastrointestinal complications, both factors that
are more likely to occur wh

ons, both factors that
are more likely to occur when CHO concentrations exceed 8 % (80 g per L) (Baker
and Jeukendrup 2014). If needed, additional CHO can be supplied through sport

3.4 Nutrition After the Marathon
Only very limited research is available how nutritional

very limited research is available how nutritional strategies may affect the
recovery from marathon running. The main nutritional goals after marathon com-
pletion involve facilitation of the recovery of ﬂuid and glycogen stores and pro-
viding nutrients to support recovery and repair mechanisms and immune function.
Depending on the level of dehydration attained during the race, adequate
rehydration may be the most signi ﬁcant nutritional strategy following marathon
running. The goal of rehydrat

y following marathon
running. The goal of rehydration is to regain ﬂuid balance, and the effectiveness of
rehydration is dependent on the amount of ﬂuid consumed as well as the electrolyte
content, primarily that of sodium. Effective rehydration can only be attained if the
amount of ﬂuid consumed covers both the ﬂuid loss that occurred during the race
(mainly in form of sweat) and additional ﬂuid losses that occur in response to
ingesting ﬂuid (primarily in form of urine). As such, it is recomme

rimarily in form of urine). As such, it is recommended to consume
at least 1.5 times the ﬂuid volume that was lost during exercise (Maughan et al.
1997). A higher sodium concentration will replace sodium sweat losses and retain
ﬂuid by reducing urinary output. Therefore, a sodium concentration of 50 –
60 mmol/L (1.1 –1.4 g/L) is considered bene ﬁcial with regards to the effectiveness
of rehydration when compared to a lower sodium concentration (20 –25 mmol/L;
0.5–0.6 g/L) (Maughan et al. 1997).

0.5–0.6 g/L) (Maughan et al. 1997).
Repletion of muscle glycogen stores typically occurs within 24 –48 h when
adequate CHO (7 –10 g/kg) are consumed (Burke et al. 2004). Because glycogen
synthesis is impaired in damaged muscle ﬁbers (Costill et al. 1988), more CHO may
be needed to restore muscle glycogen levels. However, in contrast to other events
where athletes may have to compete again shortly after the race, fast glycogen
repletion recovery should not be a high priority for mar

ion recovery should not be a high priority for marathon runners (Burke et al.
2004). Co-ingestion of protein along with may be bene ﬁcial for glycogen resyn-
thesis and may provide additional amino acids for post-exercise protein synthesis.
However, it remains unknown if these strategies actually translate into improved
recovery and/or improved performance during subsequent marathon races.

Marathon running and other prolonged endurance exercise is associated with an
increased risk of upper respiratory tract infections (URTI). Even though the patho-
physiology of URTI is not fully understood, it has been hypothesized that prolonged
heavy exertion is associated with an acute suppression of immune function
(Akerström and Pedersen 2007). Whereas results from a meta-analysis suggest that
supplementation of vitamin C may be associated with a reduction in infection rates in
populations w

th a reduction in infection rates in
populations who are exposed to severe exercise (Akerstr öm and Pedersen 2007),
prospective studies have failed to demonstrate the capacity of vitamin C supple-
mentation to attenuate the immune response to prolonged running (Peters et al.
2001). Supplementation of glutamine, an amino acid that is essential for lymphocyte
proliferation, has been associated with reduced infection rates following marathon
and ultramarathon running in one study (Castell and Newsh

ramarathon running in one study (Castell and Newsholme 1997). However,
subsequent trials have failed to con ﬁrm these effects. For other supplements,
including colostrum, which contains bovine immunoglobulins, there is no scienti ﬁc
evidence the infection risk following prolonged exerting exercise such as marathon
running can be reduced by supplementation (Akerstr öm and Pedersen 2007).
Alcohol consumption following strenuous exercise may impair muscle glycogen
synthesis and can negatively impac

muscle glycogen
synthesis and can negatively impact the post-exercise in ﬂammatory response. More
importantly, alcohol consumption may interfere with other recovery strategies
(Vella and Cameron-Smith 2010). Therefore, athletes are encouraged to refrain
from excessive alcohol consumption following the race and focus their attention on
nutritional and hydration strategies that are effective in supporting post-marathon
recovery.
3.5 Summary
Promising nutritional strategies that can be bene ﬁcial f

ng nutritional strategies that can be bene ﬁcial for marathon runners include
provision of adequate energy, carbohydrates, and protein, to address the increased
nutrient requirements of marathon training. Prolonged training in a state of low
carbohydrate or energy availability can be associated with negative health and
performance effects and should therefore be avoided by marathon runners. Both
nutritional and exercise-related factors explain why marathon runners are at par-
ticular risk of ina

y marathon runners are at par-
ticular risk of inadequate iron status. The importance of carbohydrates for marathon
performance is highlighted by the fact that pre-race strategies aimed at maximizing
muscle glycogen storage as well as the administration of additional carbohydrates
during the race are highly likely to improve marathon performance. Adequate
provision of ﬂuid and sodium is particularly important in conditions when dehy-
dration and/or sodium losses may limit performance or impact h

or sodium losses may limit performance or impact health negatively.
Among the many supplements available for marathon runners, clear scienti ﬁc
evidence for a performance bene ﬁt is only available for caffeine. Incorporating
these strategies into their training routine will allow marathon runners to become
familiarized with these strategies and test their individual responsiveness prior to
the actual race.

submaximal intensities (specific running speeds)
and the ratio of work output to oxygen
consumption (Saunders et al., 2004; Shaw et al.,

HIIT significantly reduced the oxygen cost of
running compared to MICT in endurance runners.

to critically evaluate the existing literature to
determine the effects of HIIT and MICT on running
economy (RE). The initial findings revealed that
HIIT significantly reduced the oxygen cost of
running compared to MICT in endurance runners.

lactate concentration. HIIT was particularly
effective as it enabled the body to adapt to lactate
more efficiently than most of other forms of
exercise. Individuals who engaged in HIIT
produced less lactate at similar exercise intensities
and demonstrated higher tolerance to lactate.

The limitations of this systematic review
include methodological and statistical
heterogeneity among the included studies, with
some exhibiting risk of bias due to methodological
weaknesses, such as lack of blinding in
intervention studies. Varying measurement
methods may have contributed to heterogeneous
results, and although subgroup analysis addressed
some sources of heterogeneity, individual‐level

moderators remained. Furthermore, the studies
did not account for other influencing factors, such
as environmental conditions, sleep, diet, and
psychological stress, which can affect running
economy. For instance, acute sleep deprivation can
impair performance (Craven et al., 2022), leading
to an increased heart rate and minute ventilation
during exercise (Mougin et al., 1991). Poor sleep
can also deteriorate athletic performance,
increasing ener

before and after exercise can improve endurance
and glycogen reserves (Flockhart and Larsen, 2024;
Khanna and Manna, 2005), while proper protein
supplementation aids muscle synthesis and repair
(Phillips and Van Loon, 2011). Dietary intake of
carbohydrates and fats influences fuel utilization
and running economy (Maunder et al., 2021), with
low carbohydrate

Psychological stress can also impact performance
by altering hormone levels, such as cortisol and
adrenaline (Rimmele et al., 2009; Schommer et al.,

Conclusions
The results of this study suggest that HIIT
is a more effective method for improving running
economy and delaying lactate accumulation, as
well as enhancing lactate tolerance, compared to
MICT in long‐distance runners. By training close to
the lactate threshold (Zone 2), HIIT facilitates
greater improvements in running economy and
postpones lactate accumulation in the
bloodstream. However, improvements i

lation in the
bloodstream. However, improvements in maximal
oxygen uptake (VO2max) were significantly more
pronounced with MICT than with HIIT. Further
high‐quality studies are needed to investigate
these effects in greater depth in the future.

INTRODUCTION
Rationale
Sarcopenia is a progressive skeletal muscle disorder,
characterized by reduced skeletal muscle quantity and func tion
which is associated with a range of negative health outcomes
including frailty, falls, reduced quality of life, an

luding frailty, falls, reduced quality of life, and mort ality
(
Cruz-Jentoft and Sayer, 2019; Cruz-Jentoft et al., 2019 ). In
addition to these individual health impacts, sarcopenia place s
a considerable economic burden on healthcare systems with
the associated costs in the UK estimated at £2.5 billion per year
(
Pinedo-Villanueva et al., 2019 ). Taken together, these eﬀects
highlight the need to develop treatment strategies to count eract
the deleterious consequences of sarcopenia.
Factors in

deleterious consequences of sarcopenia.
Factors including chronic inﬂammation, mitochondrial
dysfunction, and reduced satellite cell function contribu te to
the onset and progression of sarcopenia ( Ziaaldini et al., 2017 ).
Exercise training has the potential to counteract these cell ular,
molecular, and neural alterations ( Marzetti et al., 2017; Seo and
Hwang, 2020 ) with aerobic and resistance exercise capable of
inducing diﬀerential adaptations ( Hawley et al., 2014 ). Previous
work has dem

ons ( Hawley et al., 2014 ). Previous
work has demonstrated that resistance exercise has multisy stem
eﬀects, acting at both the physiological [e.g., improvements
in mitochondrial function ( Melov et al., 2007 ) and reduced
inﬂammation (Beyer et al., 2012 )] and the functional level [e.g.,
improvements in muscle strength and physical performance
(
Peterson et al., 2010; Steib et al., 2010 )]. To date there remains
no pharmacological treatment approved for the treatment of
sarcopenia and resistan

roved for the treatment of
sarcopenia and resistance exercise training is recommended as its
primary treatment (
Dent et al., 2018 ). Given the multi-factorial
nature of sarcopenia, exercise programmes for older adults li ving
with sarcopenia often involve a combination of exercise modes
(
Witham et al., 2020 ) with the aim of simultaneously improving
muscular and cardiorespiratory function ( Hurst et al., 2019a ).
Oﬀering a range of alternative exercise training approaches
which can simultaneou

exercise training approaches
which can simultaneously improve multiple outcomes (e.g.,
muscle strength, physical performance, and cardiorespirator y
ﬁtness) could help to maximize the potential of exercise as a
therapeutic strategy for older people living with sarcopenia.
High intensity interval training (HIIT) has previously been
shown to exert substantial cardio-protective eﬀects, across a
range of population groups (
Knowles et al., 2015; Hwang et al.,
2016; Batacan et al., 2017; Füzéki and B

g et al.,
2016; Batacan et al., 2017; Füzéki and Banzer, 2018; Hannan et al.,
2018; Hayes et al., 2020; Herbert et al., 2021 ). In the clinical
context, HIIT has been shown to be a safe, feasible and eﬀectiv e
therapeutic strategy in patients living with diabetes ( Little et al.,
2011), heart failure ( Angadi et al., 2015 ) and coronary artery
disease ( Warburton et al., 2005 ). From a pragmatic perspective,
HIIT can be embedded within the clinical pathway ( Way et al.,
2020) and can be delivere

al pathway ( Way et al.,
2020) and can be delivered using a range of exercise modes (e.g.,
stair climbing, stepping, cycling, walking).
Despite this, much less is known about how HIIT could
improve elements of muscular structure and function. A
recent narrative review (
Callahan et al., 2021 ) outlined several
mechanistic explanations as to why HIIT might be anabolic
in nature. These authors called for further investigation o f
HIIT in populations of diﬀerent age groups and training
status to ex

s of diﬀerent age groups and training
status to explore this phenomenon further. Moreover, they
proposed HIIT may be beneﬁcial in middle and older age
where physical conditioning (i.e., aerobic ﬁtness) and incr eased
muscle quantity were simultaneously desired. Whether HIIT
could provide the necessary improvements in muscle quantity,
quality, and strength, in addition to cardioprotective eﬀects
however, remain unclear (
Hurst et al., 2019b ). The potential for
HIIT to simultaneously induce impro

potential for
HIIT to simultaneously induce improvements in cardiometabolic
health and muscular health is an appealing strategy. However,

This scoping review provided an overview of existing literatu re
pertaining to HIIT and phenotypic characteristics of sarcopeni a.
We examined outcomes according to the revised EWGSOP
deﬁnition (
Cruz-Jentoft et al., 2019 ) to facilitate translation of
research ﬁndings into clinical practice. Firstly, the earlies t article
cited was Adamson et al. (2014) publish

cited was Adamson et al. (2014) published in 2014, which
speaks to this rapidly emerging area of research. This review
catalogs existing literature, with a view to facilitating di scussion
of research opportunities and issues that need to be addressed in
future studies.
In relation to our ﬁrst objective, which was to search the
literature for the eﬀect of HIIT on phenotypic characteristics of
sarcopenia in older adults, we observed most studies reported at
least one positive change in

least one positive change in characteristics when compared to vs.
pre-HIIT , vs. non-exercise control, or vs. MICT. In this conte xt,
19 of 20 studies reported an improvement to ≥ 1 muscle function
outcome for ≥ 1 comparisons examined (vs. pre-HIIT , vs. non-
exercise control, or vs. MICT) (
Bruseghini et al., 2019). Similarly,
twelve of 22 reported an improvement to ≥ 1 muscle quantity
outcome for ≥ 1 comparison examined, and 11 of 12 reported an
improvement to for ≥ 1 phy

nd 11 of 12 reported an
improvement to for ≥ 1 physical performance outcome for ≥ 1
comparison examined.
In relation to our second objective, training programmes
ranged in duration from 2 to 24 weeks (median = 9.5 weeks),
incorporated resistance training based HIIT , running/walk ing
HIIT , cycling HIIT , and HIIT combined with other exercise
modes (i.e., resistance training). Populations studied wer e
commonly in the 7th decade of life, and mostly living
independently. In relation to our third

ly living
independently. In relation to our third objective, muscle quantity,
or quality was most frequently studied in the included liter ature.
DEXA was the most utilized measurement method, which is in
line with the EWGSOP algorithm for sarcopenia case ﬁndings
in clinical practice (
Cruz-Jentoft et al., 2019 ). However, these
are only routinely found in research facilities and hospitals
and would likely require a referral from primary care before
an individual received a DEXA scan. Importantl

According to the revised EWGSOP deﬁnition of sarcopenia
(
Cruz-Jentoft et al., 2019 ), muscle function is primarily
considered as muscle strength. Yet, the chair stand te

idered as muscle strength. Yet, the chair stand test (or
its variations) is named as a parameter that measures muscle
strength. However, as the chair stand test relies on the abil ity
to generate force over a short period of time, this could be
considered a test of muscle power, rather than a measure of
maximal force. The term dynapenia [i.e., the age-associated
reduction in muscle strength and power (
Clark and Manini, 2012;
Manini and Clark, 2012 )] was originally used to diﬀerentiate
itself f

itself from sarcopenia ( Clark and Manini, 2008 ), which has its
roots in age-related reduced muscle mass [Greek translation
= “poverty of ﬂesh” (
Kim and Choi, 2013 )]. However, more
recent deﬁnitions and diagnoses of sarcopenia have broadened
to include muscle function. In this context, when one measur es
muscle strength using non-isometric movements (i.e., when
work occurs), force, distance, and time can be extracted, wh ich

CONCLUSIONS AND PRACTICAL
RECOMMENDATIONS
In conclusion, most studies presented herein utilized outco me
measures deﬁned by the revised EWGSOP guidelines. There
was divergence observed in exercise interventions, with HII T
interventions involving a range of exercise modes delivered in a
range of settings. Currently, there is some evidence sugges ting
HIIT may improve phenotypic characteristics of sarcopenia.
However, there are few stu

eristics of sarcopenia.
However, there are few studies investigating any form of HII T in
the very old, or those diagnosed with sarcopenia. Therefore, more
intervention studies are needed in this population to conﬁrm
this phenomenon and conﬁdently quantify the eﬀectiveness of
HIIT. In addition, we need to understand if this is a safe and
feasible training approach in this population. In a practical
context, combined interventions involving HIIT and resista nce
training are a worthy avenue for in

training are a worthy avenue for investigation as resistance
training is the most potent stimulus to increase muscle quanti ty
and studies herein showed divergent results concerning HII T
and muscle quantity. Finally, HIIT or SIT that is easy to apply
(i.e., without equipment needs, travel, specialist training, a nd
intensity monitoring such as heart rate or power output) or can
be supported virtually is likely needed to promote the transitio n

Applied Periodization: A Methodological Approach. J. Hum. Sport Exerc. Vol. 8, No. 2, pp. 350-366, 2013. Periodization represents an optimal modalit

2013. Periodization represents an optimal modality for organizing training programs in athletes, recreational and rehabilitative practitioners. The selected procedure, however, should be based on the athlete’s age, level of performance, specific goals or competition characteristics. A common theme throughout all periodization paradigms is the requirement to manipulate the entire program variables (intensity, volume, frequency, recovery periods and exercise selection) in order to progress from g

nd exercise selection) in order to progress from general to a more sport-specific training, dissipate fatigue and reduce the risk of injury. Although further scientific evidences are required, the understanding of periodization methodology including the appropriate procedure for designing sessions, microcycles and mesocycles is of paramount importance. Key words: TRAINING PLAN, PROGRAM DESIGN, MACROCYCLE, MESOCYCLE, MICROCYCLE, SESSION.

has been defined as the methodical planning and structuring of training process that involve a logical and systematic sequencing of multiple training variables (intensity, volume, frequency, recovery period and exercises) in an integrative fashion aimed to optimize specific performance outcomes at predetermined time points. Periodization should not only focus on performance but also on athlete’s development and injury prevention (Haff, 2013). Although, several periodization paradigms have been p

However, periodization should not be considered a simply training variation strategy but an appropriate sequencing and integration of different training variables involving not only volume and intensity but also frequency, recovery periods or density and exercises selection. levels of adaptation and improved performance capabilities.

4.3 Periodisation
Periodisation is the process of dividing an annual training programme into periods of
training to allow the programme to be set into manageable segments and to ensure a
correct peaking for the main competition or training objective of the year.
The process of periodisation depends on the use of the concepts of training loads
and the wave principle of t

and the wave principle of training. This information will enable better understanding of
the principal components of periodisation: training period, training cycle and training
session.
Training load
The training load consists of the quantity and quality of work. Quantity is represented
by distance of work, time of work, or number of repetitions, etc. Thus, a rowing training
session may be described as, for example, 16km in distance during which three
repetitions of ten mi

distance during which three
repetitions of ten minutes of work will be performed.
Quality is the effort exerted in the training session. It may be represented as the speed of
running, the amount of weight lifted, heart rate maintained, or, in the boat, a combination
of pressure applied on the blade and the stroke rating, etc. Thus, the example rowing
training session above may be further described as three repetitions of ten minutes of
work at a rating of 26 strokes per minute while maintaining

rating of 26 strokes per minute while maintaining a heart rate of 140 to 170.
In a systematic plan of training, the training load goes from quantity to quality. This
means that, after a period of adjusting to a new training season, the training starts
with a large quantity of a relatively low or medium quality of work to provide all-round
development and improvement in endurance capabilities.
As the training season progresses, there is a gradual increase in quality and a
corresponding decrease

increase in quality and a
corresponding decrease in quantity. This enables the development of the specific needs
of the sport of rowing and the necessary performance capabilities to achieve the training
objective.
Although this procedure is for the major part of the programme, it must be considered
as a guide because training in any period of the year is complex and must cover all
aspects of the work requirements of rowing.

The training cycle is

wave principle of training
The training cycle is a limited period of training, usually between four and eight weeks,
during which the programme is directed toward a certain training objective. Training
cycles follow the wave principle of applying alternating phases of increasing and
decreasing training load.
It has been demonstrated that this step or wave approach is more efficient than the
linear or continuous method of loading. As opposed to the continuous method, the
wave principle requires

he continuous method, the
wave principle requires that a training load increase must be followed by a decrease in
training load during which the athlete’s body is able to recover and adapt to the training
load. This enables the athlete to be subjected to progressively increasing training loads.

Introduction
This “Training Programme for Clubs” is based on The FISA Development Club
Programme distributed in 1993. Many coaches have asked for an update, but in
training methodology and rowing technique not much has changed, and the basics
stay the same. Anyhow, some training models have been improved and distribution of
time

odels have been improved and distribution of
time looks a bit different.
The difference from 1993 is the higher number of hours invested in training by the
international elite. With more than 40 hours a week in training a lot of injuries in form of
stress fractures and lower back problems occurred.
Among the lightweight rowers it looks as if the immune defense got strongly reduced
and common colds, influenza and other fever-related illnesses caused many breaks in
the training system. This is pro

ed many breaks in
the training system. This is probably a result of high training load and reduced intake
of food to keep the weight down. A problem we must address strongly in the time to
come.
In this programme we have two new appendices presenting a better programme for
flexibility and series of additional exercises to give the clubs the possibility to create a
more “all-round” training programme and avoid “disharmony” between the different
groups of muscles. Many injuries could be related to

oups of muscles. Many injuries could be related to underdevelopment in non-specific
rowing muscles (see chapter 5 – General Fitness Training).
The aim of the programme will follow the same lines as the last edition:
• Increase maximum VO2
• Increase strength endurance
• Increase maximum strength
• Higher efficiency of rowing technique
• Better flexibility and coordination

Intensity
The intensity is expressed in “heart rate” with an indicated “target zone”, based on
percentage of “maximum heart rate”. Maximum heart rate is estimated as 220 minus
age. In the programmes 200 HR is used as maximum and 180 HR as minimum.
Individual variations will occur frequently.

Indicated stroke rate
The stroke rate is closely connected to the heart rate, but has its own technical effect.
Close to the regatta season, and inside the regatta season, it is important to train in
the “stroke rate area” where we are supposed to compete.
The single sculler and the eight will use different “stroke rate areas”, and in the
programme the l

nt “stroke rate areas”, and in the
programme the lowest number is an indication for the slow boats and the highest
number for the fast boats. Weather conditions must be taken into consideration with
slower rate in headwind and upstream.
Lightweight rowers
Lightweight rowers should not use the “volume” or “maximum strength training”,
because it will increase bodyweight and muscle volume. With the “top pyramid”,
maximum strength can be improved without weight gain.

The FISA Coaching Development Programme: Handbook – Level II 59
Basic Traininfg
Methodology
Junior rowers
Junior rowers should have passed puberty and have a settled body before they start
with heavy weight training. The best period to improve muscle volume and strength
seems to be between 18 and 23 years. For younger rowers their own body weight can
be used as load. Circuit training and endurance training are to be preferred.
Women
Women can follow the same training principles as men. Their max

low the same training principles as men. Their maximum strength is
lower and muscle volume smaller, but their adaptation to endurance is as high as for
men. Some scientists insist that women recover faster from heavy endurance load
than men do.
Be careful with weight training, and take time to learn a good lifting technique.
Time requirement
To follow the programme completely from October to the end of August, you will need
approximately 650 hours of effective training. Total numbers of kilometr

s of effective training. Total numbers of kilometres on the water
are of approximately 4,000.
An international elite rower will use up to 1,500 hours/ year and row between 7 and
9,000km. Remember: less quantity needs more quality.
Reduction of the programme
School and work problems might reduce the possibility to follow the programme and
reduction will be needed. With reduction try to keep the endurance part, and give
priority to the boat training.

Terminology
To avoid misunderstanding we will explain the following “terms” used in the
programme.
Steady state
Aerobic training with metabolic balance. Energy covered 100% aerobic or with small
amount of anaerobic capacity involved, but without accumulated production of acid
lactate.
”LSD” Long Slow Distance
Training after the continuity principle to increase or mainta

ter the continuity principle to increase or maintain oxygen utilisation in the
muscle fibres recruited. Energycovered 100% aerobic.
Interval
Interval principle: Training with periodic changes between exertion and rest, or between
high and low workload (interval work).
The various types of interval training can be divided into two categories: short interval
training and long interval training.
Short interval involves work periods of up to two minutes and rests that are so short
that oxygen uptake

tes and rests that are so short
that oxygen uptake and the pulse (in the rest) does not decrease appreciably before
the start of the next work period.
Long interval involves work periods from two minutes and up to between 10 and 15
minutes, and rest lengths such that work intensity can be maintained approximately
constant during each work period.
The short interval is very important during the regatta season to keep a good quantity
of training in the right area of race velocity, and use of strok

the right area of race velocity, and use of stroke rate valid for competition.
Training after the interval principle will increase or maintain the heart’s stroke volume
(increased aerobic capacity).
Rhythm variations
Training with mainly aerobic effect, but also with some input of anaerobic energy. The
training gives a good opportunity to control and train the technique at different levels of
intensity.
Fartlek
Training according to the interval principle, of relatively long duration (8-12km),

principle, of relatively long duration (8-12km), with
improvised alteration between high and low intensity, and with the main purpose of
increasing or maintaining aerobic endurance. Gives a good opportunity to control the
technique at different levels of intensity.

Model training
Training that simulates the race condition including warming up, start proceeding
and tactic. Should be organised with other crews and made as close up to regatta
conditions as possible. (Used in connection with “supercompensation”.)
Speed training
This term is used as a description of high intensity training in preparation for regattas
(supercompensation principle.) It means mainly overpro

ercompensation principle.) It means mainly overproduction of speed (speed higher
than race speed.). This is the only specific anaerobic training in the programme. It also
has a technical element and overstimulates the muscular contraction velocity.
“Race-training: 4-2-1”
Training that stimulates race conditions, physiologically and mentally, about 60%
aerobic and 40% anaerobic with increased load. The model has also a good
technical element.
Technical “drill”:
Training with specific exercises to

nical “drill”:
Training with specific exercises to improve the rowing technique. The rowing stroke
divided into sections and trained separately followed by combined sections – up to
the full stroke.

aren’t convinced, why not give exercise a try, say

(One exercise session will not help.) As time goes

together with diet and medication.

Regular walking keeps weight

other hand, can lead to weight gain,
obesity and a higher risk of diabetes,
stroke and heart disease.

ur core muscles that run the entire

corset. When these muscles contract, they
stabilise the spine, pelvis and shoulder

remedy this weakness. Core stabilisation
exercises can be attempted progressively,
from beginner level to more

prevent injury.

Abstract Abstract
In order to create the perfect resistance training program for their athletes, coaches must master the
ability to control all variables of training over time in order to maximize physiological responses - this is a
concept known as periodization (3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 19, 21, 24, 25, 26).
Periodization was first established in Russia, after the conclusion of the 1956 Olympic games (7, 21).
Though sim

sion of the 1956 Olympic games (7, 21).
Though simple in its principle and aim, periodization is frequently misunderstood due to the hyper-
specific research that surrounds it (3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 15, 21, 23, 25). Over the last five decades, researchers
have produced a multitude of studies that look at specific variables of periodization, which this paper will
later examine, but many of them prove to be inconclusive due to uncontrollable factors outside of training
(3, 4, 7, 8, 13, 14, 19, 21). Thes

ide of training
(3, 4, 7, 8, 13, 14, 19, 21). These uncontrollable factors make it difficult to be absolute in any conclusions
surrounding the topic of periodization, though there are a number of considerations that make
periodization very valuable (25).
Periodization is of paramount importance when creating resistance training plans due to its role in the
manipulation and subsequent control of variables over time (3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 19, 21, 24, 25, 26). Without
control of variables, resistance

control of variables, resistance training becomes an aimless and non goal-oriented task (25, 43). In
comparison with non-periodized resistance programs, periodized plans prove to be significantly more
effective in strength gained, lean mass gained, and percent body fat lost (1, 5, 6, 11, 15, 25). Periodization
will likely remain a topic of controversy for a long time to come, as coaches continue to seek the most
effective combination and manipulation of training variables at the

it
difficult to be absolute in any conclusions surrounding the topic of periodization, though
there are a number of considerations that make periodization very valuable (25).
Periodization is of paramount importance when creating resistance training plans
due to its role in the manipulation and subsequent control of variables over time (3, 6, 7,
8, 9, 10, 19, 21, 24, 25, 26). Without control of variables, resistance training becomes
an aimless and non goal-oriented task (25, 43). In comparison w

d non goal-oriented task (25, 43). In comparison with non-periodized
resistance programs, periodized plans prove to be significantly more effective in
strength gained, lean mass gained, and percent body fat lost (1, 5, 6, 11, 15, 25).
Periodization will likely remain a topic of controversy for a long time to come, as
coaches continue to seek the most effective combination and manipulation of training
variables at their disposal (23).

TRAINING PRINCIPLES
General Adaptation Sy ndrome, known as GAS, states that, when exposed to
stress, three phases of adaptation will occur: the alarm phase, the resistance phase,
and the exhaustion phase (7, 23). The alarm phase occurs when the athlete will
experience mild fatigue or a decrease in performance (23). The resistance phase
occurs when the body naturally responds to the stressor by adapting with less soreness
and an improved performance (also known as supercompensation) (23).

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
erformance (also known as supercompensation) (23). Finally, if the
individual is unable to adapt to the stress, the exhaustion phase occurs (7, 23). There
are several implications of GAS principle when considering periodization for athletes;
one of the most important is the ability to regulate one’s fatigue properly over a long
period of time (7, 10, 15, 23). Fatigue management is controlled by manipulating the
training variables of volume, intensity, and frequency - which will be discussed late

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
sity, and frequency - which will be discussed later in
this paper - and their relationship to the principle of overload (25).
The principle of overload states that any individual who is exposed to training that
goes beyond normal levels of physical performance will adapt to be able to achieve that
higher level of performance in future exercise bouts (5, 11, 19, 24, 27, 28, 29). As the
GAS principle indicates, when an individual continues to make gains from an exercise
program, they will need to

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
gains from an exercise
program, they will need to introduce more challenging stimuli in order to continue in their
progression (28, 29). As muscles increase in both size and strength over time, they will
naturally be able to produce more force and thus accrue more gain (25, 28, 29). This
involves the concept of progressive overload, which states that, to continue creating

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
Yanes 4
adaptation, the individual must increase stress to the muscle over time that is
proportional to that of the progress made (5, 24, 27, 28).
In order to progressively overl oad effectively, one must properly apply the
principle of specificity to their training, which states that the adaptations that one
experiences in training are specific to the stress provided (27, 28, 29). The principle of
specificity dictates which specific adaptations that an individual will acquire through their
trai

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
that an individual will acquire through their
training, so it plays an imperative role in the overall picture of periodization (27, 28, 29).
Additionally, the specificity of exercise dictates which muscle groups and movement
patterns will be primarily developed through exercise (28). An example of this would be
a baseball pitcher addressing a weak point in his shoulder through selecting exercises
that involve the rotator cuff muscles in order to improve the circumductive nature of the
throwing m

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
improve the circumductive nature of the
throwing motion (28).
After having trained specific mov ement patterns over a sustained period of time,
the individual will adapt and will need new stimuli to continue getting stronger (20, 27,
29, 30). Variation in a resistance training program refers to the changing of variables
including weight used (intensity), volume performed, type of contraction, and speed of
contraction through different blocks of training (29). Additionally, manipulation of these

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
raining (29). Additionally, manipulation of these
variables in the short term potentially reduces stress on certain muscle groups, thereby
promoting supercompensation (27). Variation in resistance training may also create
greater adherence of the individual to their program due to the novelty behind learning
new movements (30). Variation in periodization is what allows the individual to
continually adapt without becoming stuck at significant plateaus in strength gains (20,
27, 29, 30). The princ

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
eaus in strength gains (20,
27, 29, 30). The principle of variation also directly impacts the principle of individuality,

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf

which states that each athlete may respond differently to the same stimulus based on
his or her genetic predispositions to gain strength (42). The principle of individuality
dictates that coaches should utilize variation in order to uncover what stimuli are optimal
for each athlete (42). It also says that the athlete must vary exercise selection, volume,
intensity, and frequency depending on their individual needs (42).

The fitness-fatigue model of training desc

E MODEL
The fitness-fatigue model of training describes the relationsh ip between an
athlete’s performance and their level of fatigue (44). Fatigue is defined as maladaptation
to a training stimulus which, if managed properly, can later be attributed to an increase
in performance following the GAS principle (7, 23, 44, 45). The fitness fatigue model
states that, after a significant amount of acute stress to the body, fatigue will initially
increase and performance will decrease (44, 45). After p

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
se and performance will decrease (44, 45). After proper recovery, fatigue will
decrease, and performance will increase (44, 45). After a period of time, if fatigue
accumulates beyond the individual’s recoverable capacity, overtraining will occur and
performance will significantly decrease (28, 29, 44, 45). Performance will benefit,
however, from a short-term period of overreaching, wherein an excessive amount of
stimulus is placed on the individual followed by a period of recovery (6, 8, 21, 23,

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
al followed by a period of recovery (6, 8, 21, 23, 25,
44, 45). This results in an acute increase in performance, and is typical of athletes such
as powerlifters or weightlifters who need to be at peak levels of fitness on one particular
day of the year (44, 45). This is why manipulating the variables of volume, intensity, and
frequency are of paramount importance to increasing strength (3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 19, 21,
24, 25, 26).

TERMINOLOGY: VOLUME, INTENSITY, FREQUENCY
Volume is defined as the total amount of work performed as either sets multiplied
by reps and load (tonnage), or simply as sets multiplied by reps (6, 10, 18,19, 20, 24).
Volume is an essential component of any periodization model, given that it needs to be
balanced in tandem with intensity (25). Intensity simply refers to the amount of weight
used in a given exercise (10, 18, 19, 20, 23, 25, 27, 30). Depending on the phase and
goal of a training

text:
30). Depending on the phase and
goal of a training cycle, the relationship between volume and intensity will change (25,
26). For example, if the athlete is in a hypertrophy phase (muscle-building phase),
overall volume will be higher, and intensity will be lower (10, 18, 19, 25, 26, 27). If the
athlete is in a strength or power phase (a phase wherein gaining strength or power is
the primary goal), in general, prescribed intensities will be higher and volume will be
lower (10, 18, 19, 25, 26, 27

r and volume will be
lower (10, 18, 19, 25, 26, 27).
Frequency simply refers to the amount of times per week or month that a specific
exercise is performed (6, 10, 25, 26, 27). Generally speaking, the recommended
frequencies per muscle group per week is two to three times, though this will vary
depending on individual physiological responses and variables outside of training such
as scheduling and free time available (6, 25, 26, 34, 35, 36).
The balance of volume, intensit y, and frequency are t

text:
balance of volume, intensit y, and frequency are the building blocks of any
periodized program (25, 31). Manipulating these variables within each week and month
allow athletes to aim and achieve their individual goals (25, 31, 32, 34, 25).
Recommendations for starting points are as follows: if the primary goal is hypertrophy,
10-20 sets per muscle group per week, with a 2x per week frequency, and with ⅔-¾ of

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf

total volume in the 6-12 repetition range, with the remaining volume in the 1-6 and 12-
20 repetition range (25, 31, 32, 33). If the primary goal in training is strength, frequency
and total sets remain the same, while ⅔-¾ of the volume should be in the 1-6 repetition
range and the remaining volume in the 6-20 repetition range (25, 31, 32, 33).
TERMINOLOGY: MICROCYCLES, MESOCYCLES, AND MACROCYCLES
A microcycle is defined as a short period of training, typically one to four weeks
(most of

of training, typically one to four weeks
(most often one or two) (9, 10, 18, 19, 20, 26). A mesocycle is defined as a period of
training between one to four months (9, 10, 18, 19, 20, 26). A macrocycle is defined as
a period of training between 9-12 months (9, 10, 18, 19, 20, 26). Properly planned micro
and meso cycles, which constitute the macrocycle plan, take into account volume,
intensity, and frequency in relation to the individual’s goals in training (9, 10, 18, 19, 25,
26).
MODELS OF PER

in training (9, 10, 18, 19, 25,
26).
MODELS OF PERIODIZATION - LINEAR
Linear periodization, otherwise known as Western periodization, is a model of
progression that begins with higher volumes and lower intensities across all exercises
and gradually moves towards lower volumes and higher intensities across all exercises
(2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 18, 21, 23, 24, 25). During the commencement of a
linearly periodized program, higher rep ranges, lower intensities and fewer sport-specifi

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
ranges, lower intensities and fewer sport-specific
movements (namely for individual strength athletes) should be utilized to achieve
physiological adaptations such as muscular endurance and hypertrophy (2, 8, 23, 24,
25). Both muscular hypertrophy and muscular endurance play imperative roles in

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
Yanes 8
increasing strength and power potential through increased cross-sectional area as well
as increased work capacity of the muscle fibers (2, 8, 23, 24, 25). These adaptations
will have great carryover to further adaptations such as strength and power in later
phases of training where more specific movements will be used (for individual strength
sport athletes) and lower overall volume will be accumulated (2, 8, 23, 24, 25).
It is important to recognize that linear periodization, as well as

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
to recognize that linear periodization, as well as all other models of
periodization, were created to be adapted to each athlete’s sport-specific requirements
(25). An example of this is a model of linear periodization that begins with a volume
phase, where intensities are low and volume is high, transitions into a strength phase,
where volume decreases and intensity increases, and ends with a power phase, where
both intensity and volume decrease (21, 23, 24, 25). This could apply to an athlete

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
(21, 23, 24, 25). This could apply to an athlete such
as a football player, who needs to transfer maximal power adaptations into the start of
the season, but who also needs to reduce fatigue at the same time by decreasing
volume and intensity over time (21, 23, 24, 25). This kind of model would not apply to a
strength athlete such as a powerlifter, who needs to continue working with higher
intensities and decreased volumes leading up to a taper prior to competition (21, 23, 24,
25).
Linear peri

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf

prior to competition (21, 23, 24,
25).
Linear periodization is not without its limitations, however. Given the long phasic
nature of the linear model, certain adaptations, such as muscular hypertrophy, are
difficult to maintain in later phases of training (21, 23). This is likely due to a disuse of
the adaptation achieved over a long period of time (21, 23). Additionally, linear
periodization does not take into account the in-season taxes to the athlete’s recovery;

athletes are not able to ‘peak’ a particular adaptation during their season due to fatigue
accumulated from their sport (21, 23, 25).
MODELS OF PERIODIZATION - BLOCK
Block periodization is a training model that divides the macrocycle into 3-4
mesocycles (blocks) that are each designated to achieve specific adaptations (2, 6, 8, 9,
14, 21, 23, 25). Though block periodization shares many elements with linear
periodization, such as varying volumes and intensities, the periods of time (the
m

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
olumes and intensities, the periods of time (the
mesocycles) in which specific adaptations are focused are much shorter; in linear
periodization, mesocycles typically last several months, whereas in block periodization,
mesocycles last 4-6 weeks (2, 6, 8, 9, 14, 21, 23, 25). This allows athletes who need to
be in peak condition multiple times a year, such as a powerlifter or sprinter, to plan
these shorter blocks based on competition dates (25). An example of a block-periodized
program would beg

text:
An example of a block-periodized
program would begin with a higher volume, lower intensity block, and would continue
with a lowered volume, higher intensity block, culminating in a taper (a period of time to
decrease either volume, intensity, or both in order to supercompensate) to peak
performance (6, 8, 21, 23, 25). Outside of the shorter mesocycle plans, block
periodization is similar to linear periodization in its fundamental elements (2, 6, 8, 9, 21,
23, 25).

MODELS OF PERIODIZATION - UNDULATING
Undulating periodization is a form of periodization that utilizes more frequent
changes to volume, intensity, and repetition ranges (3, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16,

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
Yanes 10
17, 22, 23, 25). Daily undulating periodization (DUP) changes these variables on a daily
basis (throughout the microcycle), while weekly undulating periodization changes these
variables every week (5, 15, 25). Like block periodization, DUP and WUP attempt to
eliminate the potential downfalls of disuse to muscular adaptation that linear
periodization creates, and like linear periodization, undulating programs follow a
progression of focusing on hypertrophy, then strength, and finally pow

source_path: C:\Users\26318\Desktop\马拉松助手\uploaded_docs\Periodization for Massive Strength Gains.pdf
text:
ing on hypertrophy, then strength, and finally power (5, 15, 21, 23,
25). An example of a DUP progression would be training hypertrophy on the first day of
the week, then strength two days later, and finally hypertrophy another two days later
(5, 15, 21, 23, 25). A WUP model would follow this same progression, except in a
weekly instead of daily progression (5, 15, 21, 23, 25).

Though there are a multitude of studies comparing the popular mo

periodization, the answer as to the question of which model is best remains uncertain
(25). Several studies have directly compared the effects on gaining strength using linear
periodization against daily and weekly undulating periodization (3, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12, 13,
15, 16, 23, 25, 37). In a number of these studies, the groups that utilized undulating
periodization over short (4-6 weeks) and long (12+ weeks) periods of time were shown
to i

to increase their overall strength at a greater rate than groups that utilized linear

concluded that there were no differences in strength gains, provided that total volume

comparisons between block-periodized programs and linear-periodized programs (2, 8,

9, 21, 23). Some of these studies conclude that block-periodized models result in

跑步生物力学与常见运动损伤预防
### 1. 跑步步态周期与生物力学基础
跑步是一种周期性的双脚交替着地运动，其基本单元为步态周期，通常定义为同一侧足部连续两次触地的时间间隔。一个完整的步态周期可划分为两个主要阶段：支撑相和摆动相。在马拉松配速下，优秀业余跑者的支撑相约占整个步态周期的60%，摆动相占40%左右；随速度增加，支撑相占比会进一步缩短。深入理解支撑相内的力学事件是预防损伤的基础。
支撑相可细分为四个功能性子相。初始接触指足部与地面发生第一次接触的瞬间，此时地面反作用力开始从零上升。接下来的承重期是身体重量快速加载到支撑腿的阶段，其特征是膝关节屈曲约20°-25°以缓冲冲击，踝关节从轻微跖屈转为背屈，足弓在载荷下轻度下降以吸收能量。该阶段结束时，垂直地面反作用力达到第一个峰值，约为体重的2.0-2.5倍，与撞击负荷密切相关。

能量。该阶段结束时，垂直地面反作用力达到第一个峰值，约为体重的2.0-2.5倍，与撞击负荷密切相关。支撑中期是单腿支撑体重并控制重心前移的阶段，髋、膝、踝关节进入更大幅度的屈曲，此时下肢肌群通过离心-向心转换来稳定关节，垂直地面反作用力短暂下降至约体重的1.5倍，随后在离地期再次上升，形成由跖屈肌群主动"推蹬"产生的第二峰值，同样可达2.5倍体重以上，推动身体进入摆动相。
关键关节角度在触地时具有高度重复的典型范围。初始接触时，下肢几何形态决定了负荷模式：膝关节通常呈15°-20°屈曲以分散冲击力，髋关节约屈曲30°-35°；踝关节角度则因触地模式不同而异，后跟触地者多呈5°-10°背屈，前掌触地者则呈15°-30°跖屈。支撑中期膝屈角峰值可达35°-45°，此时髋内收角度若超过15°且伴随膝外翻，则被视为与多种过劳性损伤高度关联。垂直地面反作用力曲线在后跟跑者中呈现典型的"双峰"形态，且常在第一峰之前出现一个仅持续数十毫秒的冲击峰，其斜率（即垂直平均加载率，VALR）是衡量冲击强度的核心指标。而前掌跑者的曲线趋于平滑的单峰，冲击峰通常消失，这一差异对后续损伤风险有深远影响。

击强度的核心指标。而前掌跑者的曲线趋于平滑的单峰，冲击峰通常消失，这一差异对后续损伤风险有深远影响。
### 2. 足部触地模式：后跟、中足、前掌
根据足部最先接触地面的解剖区域，跑步触地模式可分为后跟触地（RFS）、中足触地（MFS）和前掌触地（FFS）。这一分类建立在Lieberman等人在《自然》杂志上发表的经典研究基础上，其后续研究证实不同模式会引发截然不同的下肢在体力学响应。
从生物力学差异来看，后跟触地者在触地瞬间足部位于身体重心前方较远处，形成膝关节被动锁死和更大的制动力矩。其垂直地面反作用力曲线会出现明显的冲击峰，垂直平均加载率通常高达70-90 BW/s（即每秒承受体重70-90倍的加载速度）。与之对比，中足触地时前掌和后跟近乎同时落地，冲击峰幅度减小，VALR降至约30-50 BW/s。前掌触地的跑者则利用足弓、跟腱和腓肠肌-比目鱼肌复合体的离心收缩来缓冲，冲击峰基本消失，VALR可低至20 BW/s以下。然而，这并非没有代价：前掌触地显著增加了踝关节跖屈力矩和跟腱应力，同时足弓和跖骨头的负荷大幅提升。

。然而，这并非没有代价：前掌触地显著增加了踝关节跖屈力矩和跟腱应力，同时足弓和跖骨头的负荷大幅提升。
在受伤风险差异方面，回顾性研究显示习惯后跟触地的跑者膝关节损伤发生率更高，而前掌触地群体中跖骨应力性骨折、跟腱病和足底筋膜炎的比例有所上升。Daoud等对哈佛大学越野队的研究发现，后跟触地者的反复应力性损伤总体风险是前掌触地者的2.6倍，但这是观察性数据，无法排除训练特征等混杂因素。目前没有高质量随机对照试验证明强制改变触地模式能降低整体损伤率。
因此，关于转换触地模式必须极其谨慎。对于无严重损伤且长期采用后跟触地的业余跑者，突然切换为前掌落地会使跟腱和足底筋膜承载的应力突增，极易诱发新的损伤。若确实因反复膝痛需在中短期内调整负荷分布，建议优先采用中足触地作为过渡，并在转换期间将跑量降低40%-50%，逐步强化小腿三头肌和足内在肌，切不可在未经力量储备的情况下强行纠正。
### 3. 步频、步幅与损伤风险
步频（每分钟步数）与步幅是跑步效率与损伤风险调控的核心杠杆。

### 3. 步频、步幅与损伤风险
步频（每分钟步数）与步幅是跑步效率与损伤风险调控的核心杠杆。早在2011年，Heiderscheit等发表的开创性研究即通过运动学与运动力学建模证实，将跑者的自然步频提升5%-10%，可在不改变跑步速度的情况下，显著降低步幅，进而引发一系列生物力学获益：髋关节内收力矩降低8%，膝关节屈曲力矩降低15%，胫骨近端前剪力也明显减小，提示胫骨应力损伤风险下降。进一步的计算显示，步频提高10%可使胫骨前侧反复应力降低10%以上。
这些改变的本质在于缩短触地时质心与足的位置距离，从而减小刹车效应（Braking Impulse）。刹车效应是指脚落地时因相对地面向前移动而产生指向后方的地面反作用力冲量，它对推进无益，反而增加了下肢的制动负荷和垂直冲击波。缩短步幅可让足部更接近身体正下方触地，膝关节在初始接触时更加屈曲，冲击力吸收更依赖肌肉而非骨骼，垂直加载率随之降低。
优化的步频常被表述为每分170-180步，但这一数值并非普适标准。

优化的步频常被表述为每分170-180步，但这一数值并非普适标准。精英马拉松运动员因步幅较长，配速在3:00/公里时步频可维持在180-190步/分；而普通跑者在6:00/公里配速时若强行达到180步/分，反而会使步幅过度缩短并增加代谢消耗。个体最佳步频取决于身高、腿长、跑步经验和弹性势能利用效率。通过节拍器或带节拍反馈的运动手表，可将步频逐步向优化值靠近。安全调整方案推荐"5%规则"：先测试当下舒适配速下的平均步频，将目标步频定在提高5%左右，每周进行2-3次短距离的节拍跑步训练，同时注意倾听身体对踝、膝负荷变化的反馈，配合力量训练，4-6周后再考虑是否进一步上调。
### 4. 常见跑步损伤及其生物力学成因
基于生物力学缺陷的过劳性损伤是马拉松跑者中断训练的主因，五种典型病症的力学成因如下：
髌股疼痛综合征（跑者膝）是发生率最高的跑步损伤，占比可达20%以上。其核心生物力学机制为髋外展肌（臀中肌为主）与外旋肌力量不足，导致支撑期股骨过度内旋和内收，造成膝关节动态外翻姿态。

机制为髋外展肌（臀中肌为主）与外旋肌力量不足，导致支撑期股骨过度内旋和内收，造成膝关节动态外翻姿态。Willson与Davis等人的前瞻性研究证实，动态膝外翻角度每增加1°，跑者膝发生风险明显升高。此外，大腿外展肌等长力减弱使骨盆不稳，间接增加了髌股关节面侧方压力，加重软骨磨损与疼痛。
髂胫束摩擦综合征多表现为膝外侧痛，炎症来源于髂胫束远端与股骨外侧髁的反复摩擦。臀中肌薄弱导致的Trendelenburg姿态（支撑侧骨盆下沉）使髂胫束被动拉长并绷紧，在膝关节30°屈伸时产生最大摩擦。同时，习惯于大步幅、低步频的跑者因触地时间延长，髂胫束反复摩擦的周期更多，诱发风险上升。
跟腱病源于肌腱承受的重复机械应力超过修复速率。过度旋前是主要生物力学危险因素之一，当距下关节旋前幅度过大时，跟腱的牵拉力线发生改变，导致肌腱局部应力集中。同时，踝关节背屈活动度受限（如被动背屈小于10°）使支撑期跟腱必须在更短的长度内承受更大的冲击载荷，小腿三头肌高度紧张更会减少肌腱的弹性势能储存能力，加速退行性变。
足底筋膜炎的典型表现为晨起第一步剧痛，其力学成因与足弓塌陷及后表链紧张密不可分。

足底筋膜炎的典型表现为晨起第一步剧痛，其力学成因与足弓塌陷及后表链紧张密不可分。当胫骨后肌力量不足或弹簧韧带支持性下降时，足弓在支撑期过度拉长，足底筋膜重复性受到牵拉和微小撕裂。同时，腓肠肌与比目鱼肌柔韧性丧失会限制踝关节背屈，迫使跖趾关节代偿性背伸以维持推进，通过"卷扬机效应"进一步牵拉足底筋膜起点，引起跟骨附着点的反复炎症和退化性变。
胫骨应力综合征（外胫夹）的本质是胫骨骨膜反复受到过载而发炎。典型危险因素包括距下关节过度内旋（舟骨下沉试验≥10 mm）和训练量骤增。过度内旋使比目鱼肌和趾长屈肌在胫骨内侧附着区域产生过强的牵张力，叠加因突然增加跑量导致的骨骼修复不及，极易诱发骨髓水肿乃至应力性骨折。女性跑者因"女运动员三联征"风险，肌肉吸收冲击的能力下降，发生率显著高于男性。
### 5. 损伤预防策略
构建系统化的预防策略，应从负荷监控、肌肉功能、装备管理与恢复再生四维度入手。
负荷监控是预防的核心。ACWR（Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio）即过去一周的急性负荷（如跑量公里数或训练负荷积分）与前四周平均慢性负荷的比值。

力量训练应聚焦于臀大肌、臀中肌、核心肌群和小腿三头肌。每周2次、每次20-30分钟的专门训练即足以产生保护效应。推荐动作包括单腿臀桥、侧卧蚌式开合、单腿罗马尼亚硬拉和提踵。这些练习旨在增强冠状面骨盆稳定性和对地冲击缓冲能力。研究显示，8周的臀中肌强化训练可使跑步时髋内收角度降低约3°，显著改善膝外翻。
跑鞋轮换是一项被证据支持的特异性措施。Malisoux等人于2015年在《英国运动医学杂志》发表前瞻性随机对照研究，发现同时轮换使用多双不同构造跑鞋的跑者，与单一穿同一型号跑鞋者相比，在22周随访期内总损伤风险降低39%。

柔韧性与动态热身及恢复手段是保持训练连续性的保障。跑前应开展动态拉伸（如直腿行军步、蠕虫行走）、迷你弹力带激活臀肌以及轻量跑步技术操，避免静态拉伸超过20秒。训练后重视睡眠时长（至少7-8小时）与蛋白质摄入（每千克体重1.2-1.6克），并可采用泡沫轴放松大腿前侧与小腿后部，每次肌群持续按压30秒，以降低肌筋膜紧张对骨骼的持续牵拉力。
### 6. 自我评估方法
跑者可通过简单而系统的方法在家进行动态评估与风险判断。
动态评估推荐单腿深蹲测试和跳跃落地质量观察。面对镜子，双手叉腰，单腿缓慢下蹲至45°-60°膝屈角，观察能否保持骨盆水平、膝关节与第二脚趾方向一致且无过度内倾。若出现明显膝内扣、躯干侧倾或骨盆塌陷，提示臀中肌与核心控制薄弱，受伤风险较高。

步态分析中最简便的是湿足测试：双足浸水后在报纸或深色地板上站立，根据足弓印判断足弓类型；但静止状态下仅提供解剖结构信息，关键要结合跑步时是否出现过度旋前，可拍摄慢动作视频观察跟骨外翻角度。
疼痛监测是防止轻微负荷反应升级为结构性损伤的最后防线。训练中应采用NRS（数字评分法）0-10分逐日记录疼痛强度。危险信号不是0-2分的轻微不适，而是训练中疼痛是否≥3分或呈现"脉冲性递增"——例如跑步开始时痛感为3，1公里后消失，但在停跑休息后再次出现并加重，或次日清晨僵痛明显。此类疼痛规律暗示组织尚处于可逆应激期，但已需调整负荷。此外，若疼痛导致不得不改变跑步姿态（如出现跛行），或出现夜间痛、静息痛，则必须停止跑步并寻求诊治。
何时就医 vs 自我调整：若疼痛可随热身消失，且NRS<3，ACWR正常，可通过减少跑量50%、加入水中跑步与强化力量训练进行自我调整观察两周。

马拉松减量训练与赛前策略 (Tapering & Pre-Race Strategy)
### 1. 减量训练的定义与生理原理
减量（taper）指赛前1-4周通过系统性降低训练负荷，让身体从长期训练积累的疲劳中恢复，从而在比赛日达到巅峰状态。其生理机制核心是消除训练疲劳与保留/强化适应：训练量下降使肌糖原储备得以超量恢复，肌糖原含量可从正常水平的约100-120 mmol/kg升高至150-200 mmol/kg，显著延长马拉松后半程供能；肌肉微损伤修复完成，肌酸激酶（CK）等损伤标志物回落至正常范围，睾酮/皮质醇比值回升，反映合成代谢环境改善；血液指标如血红蛋白、血容量趋于稳定，运氧能力优化；同时神经肌肉效率提升，跑步经济性改善。Mujika & Padilla (2003) 的经典综述指出，设计合理的减量可提升耐力运动成绩0.5%-6%，平均约3%，这一幅度足以在马拉松中将2小时30分的成绩提高约4分30秒。

耐力运动成绩0.5%-6%，平均约3%，这一幅度足以在马拉松中将2小时30分的成绩提高约4分30秒。减量的关键在于三要素的调整比例：训练量（volume，总跑量）应大幅减少，是减量的核心；训练强度（intensity）必须维持或略微增加，以保持训练的积极生理适应；训练频率（frequency）不应降低，保持原有的训练日数，以维持神经肌肉协调模式和节奏感。
### 2. 减量策略类型
减量策略主要有三种类型。线性减量（Linear Taper）指每周以恒定比例降低训练量，例如每周递减15%-20%，操作简单，适合经验较少的大众跑者，但因前期降幅温和，在较短减量周期（如2周）内总恢复可能不足。指数减量（Exponential Taper）是在减量初期将训练量快速下降，后期趋于平缓；又可根据下降速度分为快衰减指数减量与慢衰减指数减量，后者在最初几天内依然保留较多训练量，随后逐步减少。Bosquet等人(2007)的元分析显示，指数型慢衰减减量对成绩提升最为有效，因为它能在减量前期维持较高训练应激，防止能力消退，随后给予充分恢复。

型慢衰减减量对成绩提升最为有效，因为它能在减量前期维持较高训练应激，防止能力消退，随后给予充分恢复。阶梯减量（Step Taper）是一次性将训练量降至某个平台并保持，常见的是在减量期前段保持较高训练量，然后突然大幅降低，这种策略较生硬，可能造成恢复不均衡。精英跑者多采用指数型减量，以保持高质量的专项强度训练，而大众跑者更适合线性减量或简化的慢衰减指数减量，平衡恢复与能力维持。无论哪种策略，总训练量在减量期通常需减少40%-60%。
### 3. 减量期训练量、频率与强度的具体建议
减量并非按比例缩减一切，而应有重点地调控。跑量缩减：以减量前最大周跑量为基准，赛前2周将跑量削减至正常的60%-70%，赛前1周继续降至40%-50%。例如周跑量80公里的跑者，倒数第二周可跑48-56公里，最后一周跑32-40公里。训练频率：保持原有的每周训练日数，若平时一周跑5-6天，减量期不应改为3-4天；取消跑休日反而容易扰乱身体节律，产生"不练的不安感"。强度维持：减量期的精华在于"减量不减强度"。间歇跑和节奏跑等关键课次必须维持目标配速甚至比赛配速，但缩短主课距离与组数。

### 4. 赛前碳水加载 (Carbohydrate Loading)
碳水加载是通过增加肌糖原储备来推迟马拉松后半程"撞墙"的核心营养手段。经典的Akerlund方案要求赛前7天先进行3天低碳水饮食（＜100克/天）配合强度训练以消耗糖原，再连续3天高碳水（8-10克/公斤/天）并休息，达到超量补偿。

### 5. 赛前 7 天逐日执行清单
D-7：轻松跑+技术练习，总距离控制在正常轻松跑的70%，检查装备并开始关注饮水，保证7-8小时睡眠。

马拉松比赛策略、配速规划与赛道执行
### 1. 配速策略类型与选择
马拉松配速策略直接影响能量代谢效率与运动表现，运动生理学界通常将其归纳为四种核心模式：匀速配速（Even）、负分段（Negative Split）、正分段（Positive Split）和抛物线型（Parabolic）。
匀速配速指全程以几乎恒定的速度完成比赛，其生理学基础在于实现最大的有氧代谢稳态，延迟乳酸堆积和糖原耗竭的出现。这种策略能将心率和摄氧量的漂移（VO₂ drift）控制在最小范围，从而降低后半程的生理代价。对于拥有稳定能量供应和精确配速感的精英跑者，匀速策略是打破世界纪录最常见的选择。例如，基普乔格在2018年柏林马拉松创造当时世界纪录时，前半程用时1小时01分06秒，后半程仅用时1小时00分33秒，几乎呈现出完美的匀速甚至轻微负分段特征。
负分段指后半程速度比前半程更快，需要在比赛前半程有意识地压住速度，为后半程储备糖原和神经驱动力。它的生理优势在于能够最大化地利用脂肪氧化供能比例在前半程的作用，并在后半程调动无氧储备实现强力冲刺。

text:
它的生理优势在于能够最大化地利用脂肪氧化供能比例在前半程的作用，并在后半程调动无氧储备实现强力冲刺。这种策略对配速控制能力和心理韧性要求极高，多见于经验丰富、目标明确的竞技跑者。Haney与Mercer（1994）在对奥运会马拉松选手的配速模式分析中发现，成功跑出个人最佳成绩的运动员更倾向于采用负分段或接近负分段的策略。
正分段则是前半程快、后半程慢的一种模式，其本质常常是生理储备的过早消耗。大量研究显示，大众跑者普遍无意识地执行正分段策略。Ely等人（2007）在对波士顿马拉松等大型赛事数万名跑者的配速数据进行分析后指出，过快的起跑速度是导致正分段和撞墙现象的核心诱因。从能量系统看，正分段使跑者过早在高糖原消耗区运动，加速肌糖原排空，导致30公里后严重的代谢危机。然而，在某些条件下，如气温骤升或赛道前段以下坡为主时，刻意采用轻微的正分段（主动调节而非崩盘形成的掉速）也可作为一种保守策略。
抛物线型配速表现为起跑较快、中段稳定、尾段可能略有回升的U形曲线，常见于精英选手在战术性比赛中。起跑阶段的快是为了抢占有利位置和摆脱集团，中段进入团队合作或巡航状态，末段再次加速决胜。

精英跑者与大众跑者的策略差异根本上源于生理储备和训练精细度的不同。精英跑者可以维持极高的速度而不触发早发性乳酸堆积，使其有能力执行匀速或负分段策略；大众跑者因最大摄氧量和乳酸阈相对较低，若效仿精英的起跑节奏，极易落入配速管理失误的陷阱。因此，大众跑者应将目标配速策略从"希望跑到的成绩"切换到"依据VDOT和训练数据计算出的现实结果"，并强制将前5公里配速降低5-10秒/公里。
### 2. 目标配速的科学设定方法
设定实际可行的全马目标配速，需综合多种科学方法，而非简单臆测。最经典的生理学工具是Jack Daniels开发的VDOT跑力值系统。VDOT是基于跑者在某一距离上的最佳表现所推算出的有氧能力当量，用它可以从近期的10公里或半马成绩精准换算全马预期配速。例如，一位10公里成绩为45分钟的跑者，其VDOT值约为42，对应全马预期成绩约为3小时24分（配速4分50秒/公里）。

训练数据外推法是第二个重要支柱。在高质量长距离跑（如30-35公里）中记录稳态心率与配速的关系，可用于推演比赛配速。具体做法是绘制配速-心率回归曲线，找到心率位于储备心率百分比（%HRR）75%-82%区间的对应速度，该区间通常为个体乳酸阈的临界区域，也是马拉松竞赛的可持续上限。如果跑者在一次32公里的马拉松配速跑中，以82%HRR心率维持4分55秒配速且未出现大幅心率漂移，那么此配速即为合理的起点。
心率策略提供了实时监控工具。依据Karvonen公式（目标心率=静息心率+目标强度×储备心率），马拉松竞赛通常对应%HRR的75%-84%。精英跑者常在80%-85%HRR区间稳定输出，大众跑者则建议锚定在75%-80%区间，避免超出乳酸阈。

天气和赛道修正是确保目标配速现实化的关键外部校准。Ely等人（2007）基于大量马拉松数据建立了温度对成绩影响的模型：当气温从最佳区间（精英选手3-8°C，大众跑者5-10°C）每升高5°C，全马成绩会下降约1.5%-3%，配速需自然放慢5-15秒/公里。高湿度会抑制汗液蒸发，使体温调节效率降低，当露点温度超过15°C时，配速应额外减慢3-5秒/公里。赛道总爬升每增加30米，相当于全马总时间增加约40-60秒。跑者需将温度、湿度和累计爬升三项修正系数叠加至原始VDOT配速上，形成"环境调整后的执行配速"。

0-5公里：生理起航段。

5-21公里：稳态巡航段。此段应使身体完全进入有氧脂肪-碳水化合物混合供能的稳态。呼吸节奏稳定，配速可微调至目标值，并锁定心率在预设的马拉松强度区间（如80%-84%HRR）。RPE应稳定在14-15（费力感轻微但可持续）。该阶段的生理挑战是防止"心率漂移"导致过早触及阈值，因此需通过每5公里补给水和能量胶来维持血浆容量与血糖。

### 4. 能量补给与配速的协同
能量补给并非孤立的营养行为，而是配速策略得以执行的生理燃料基础，二者必须精确协同。
赛前碳水加载需与配速目标匹配。目标配速越快（例如<4分30秒/公里），糖原消耗速率越高，赛前糖原超量补偿越要充分。经典的Ahlborg方案建议在赛前36-48小时采用高碳水饮食（每日7-10克/公斤体重），同时减量训练。对于冲击3小时以内的大众精英跑者，仅靠肝糖原和肌糖原储备至多维持约90分钟高强度运动，因此赛前加载可将肌糖原从通常的100-120 mmol/kg湿肌提升至180-200 mmol/kg，直接与后程不掉速能力挂钩。

赛中补给计划的核心在于糖原节约与外源性碳水氧化。以马拉松配速跑步时，总碳水化合物氧化速率约在2.0-3.5克/分钟。若不补充，约在70-90分钟后即开始动用结构性蛋白质并面临糖原耗竭风险。科学建议每30-45分钟摄入一份含碳水量25-30克的能量胶，确保每小时补充60-90克碳水化合物，并使用葡萄糖与果糖（2:1比例）的"多重可运输型"混合物，可将外源性碳水氧化率提升至每小时90克以上（Jeukendrup, 2010），从而有效节约内源性糖原。对于4小时30分完赛的跑者，其每分钟绝对功率较低，碳水消耗速率可能仅1.8克/分钟，补给频率可稍缓；而对3小时以内的跑者，则必须严格执行每30分钟一次的补给规划，否则配速极易在30公里后崩塌。

起跑过快综合征（Mismanaged Pacing Syndrome）是大众跑者最普遍的代谢灾难。其生理根源是激情引发的高儿茶酚胺水平，短暂掩盖了真实的生理需求，导致前5公里配速超过目标15秒/公里以上。Ely等人（2007）的大数据证据显示，前5公里配速偏差超过建议值8%的跑者，其完赛时间的正分段差值可高达8-12分钟。

高温环境下的热适应训练与补水策略
### 1. 高温对马拉松运动表现的影响
高温环境是马拉松运动中最严峻的外部挑战之一，其对运动表现的削弱涉及多层次的生理机制。当环境温度超过最佳竞赛区间（通常为5-10°C），核心体温的加速升高成为表现下降的核心驱动力。运动中骨骼肌产热使核心温度迅速上升，在凉爽环境下，身体可通过辐射、对流和汗液蒸发有效散热；但在高温尤其是高湿条件下，皮肤-环境温度梯度减小或反转，导致干热交换受阻，而高湿度又大幅抑制汗液蒸发效率，使核心体温呈现不可遏制的线性攀升。一旦核心温度达到约40°C的临界点，中枢神经系统便会启动保护性抑制，降低运动单位的招募频率，表现为主观疲劳感剧增和步速的被动下降。
Ely等人2007年在《Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise》发表的里程碑式研究，汇总了波士顿、纽约等七大马拉松赛事超过二十年、近千万条完赛成绩数据，系统分析了环境温度对马拉松表现的影响。

波士顿、纽约等七大马拉松赛事超过二十年、近千万条完赛成绩数据，系统分析了环境温度对马拉松表现的影响。该研究揭示，当气温从5°C逐步升高时，所有完赛群体的成绩均出现规律性衰退：环境温度每升高5°C，全马完赛时间平均增加1.5%-3%，且这一影响在较慢完赛者（如4小时以上）中更为显著，精英选手虽受影响较小，但同样存在成绩放缓。例如，在10-15°C区间内精英跑者的成绩接近最佳，而一旦温度升至20-25°C，成绩平均放慢2%-3%，部分慢速跑者甚至可达5%以上。
伴随高温出现的还有心血管漂移（Cardiovascular Drift）现象。在持续长时间、恒定强度的运动中，即使配速不变，心率也会随时间推移而逐渐升高，而每搏输出量下降。这一方面源于脱水导致的血浆容量减少和静脉回流下降，另一方面是皮肤血管舒张需求与肌肉供血的竞争加剧。热应激下，皮肤血流量可增加至心输出量的20%-30%，以促进散热，但这也意味着骨骼肌灌注相对不足，迫使心脏以更高的跳动频率维持心输出量，同时最大摄氧量（VO₂max）出现可测得的下降。

热应激还会深刻影响能量代谢。高温可直接升高肌糖原的利用速率，并促进循环儿茶酚胺释放，使肌糖原分解加速；同时，内脏血流减少导致肝脏糖异生能力下降，加上恶心、食欲抑制等消化功能紊乱，糖分补充困难，极易引发早期糖原耗竭，形成"撞墙"提前。此外，高温对神经肌肉接头和肌细胞膜兴奋性的直接影响不可忽视，大量出汗所致的电解质紊乱（尤其是钠和钾的失衡）可降低肌肉的力量输出和协调性，使跑步经济性进一步受损，抽筋风险骤增。
不同体能水平及性别对高温的耐受性存在差异。最大摄氧量较高、训练有素的跑者通常拥有更大的血浆容量和更敏感的出汗调节能力，但仍需面对更高的绝对产热量和更易出现的脱水速率。在性别维度上，女性的体表面积与体重比通常更大，有利于干热交换，但其出汗阈值较高、最大出汗率较低，更依赖于循环系统的散热调节。

### 2. 热适应的生理机制与益处
热适应是通过系统、反复的热暴露使机体发生一系列适应性改变，从而提升在高温下运动和生存能力的生理过程。其基础机制由Sawka、Cheuvront等学者在多项综述中系统阐述，核心变化在7-14天内即可取得质的飞跃。
血浆容量扩张是首要适应。仅在热暴露开始的第3-5天，血容量即可增加10%-15%，这得益于肾素-血管紧张素-醛固酮系统激活、抗利尿激素的适度释放以及血浆蛋白质合成增加。扩容后的血液循环系统不仅增强了每搏输出量和心输出量储备，还能够更好地同时支持中枢循环与皮肤散热需求，显著延缓心血管漂移的发生，使运动中心率降低、心脏工作更经济。
出汗功能的重新编程是热适应的另一标志。热适应后，出汗阈值显著降低——即在更低的平均体温下就开始出汗，同时最大出汗率可提升30%-50%，且汗腺分布更为均匀。这使得身体对核心温度的微小上升就能做出迅速反应，散热效率大幅增强。

热适应对最大摄氧量（VO₂max）的影响在热环境中尤为明显。未适应者进入高温环境时，VO₂max可骤降5%-15%；而完成热适应后，这种衰减可被部分逆转，通常能将损失缩小至3%-7%。这很大程度上得益于血容量扩张和心血管稳定性的提升。此外，热适应也能改善肌肉氧化代谢的底物利用，减少对糖原的依赖，并保护肌肉力量和中枢驱动的完整性。心理层面的热耐受提升同样不容低估：反复热暴露会降低对热不适的主观敏感度，削弱因燥热产生的情绪波动和放弃意念。
### 3. 热适应训练方案
科学的热适应方案需根据赛程、个体条件和可用资源量身定制，其核心原理是使核心体温每日维持38.5-39.5°C区间并持续一定时间，以激发细胞和系统层面的适应性信号。经典方案由Sawka及Armstrong等人的工作提炼而来，可分为短期方案、完整方案和维持方案。
短期方案（7天）适用于时间紧迫的跑者，重点是每日进行60-90分钟的中低强度热暴露训练。训练强度应控制在心率储备的55%-65%，或以RPE 12-14"轻松至有点吃力"为准。

当无法频繁进入自然高温环境时，被动热适应是备受推崇的替代手段，尤其适合精英跑者和赛前精细调控。其典型操作是：运动后在热水浴（40°C）中浸泡30-40分钟，或进入桑拿房（70-80°C）15-25分钟，期间可补充少量水分。研究证实，连续6-7天、每天运动后立即进行30分钟热水浴，核心体温可保持升高约1.0-1.5°C，同样能够诱导血浆容量扩张和出汗功能改善。甚至可采用"运动后不关风扇、穿多层衣物维持体温"的方式延长热暴露信号。虽然被动适应对出汗率和心血管的刺激略逊于运动热适应，但它是很好的补充和维持手段。
热适应的维持与时间线：热适应的生理效应消退速度相对较快，若不再接受热刺激，血浆容量扩张在停训后约5-7天开始消退，出汗增益可持续约2-3周才逐渐减弱，因此建议赛前热适应的最后冲刺应在赛前3周开始，并在赛前最后一周安排2-3次维持性热暴露。原则是每3-5天需要一次有效热刺激，否则渐进式丢失。对于无法前往热带的跑者，家庭模拟热适应尤为实用：穿着多层保暖衣物在无风扇的室内训练，适度调高室温或使用暖气，确保运动过程中大量出汗和体感温度升高。

### 4. 比赛中补水与电解质策略
水分和电解质管理是高温马拉松的生命线。脱水程度与运动表现下降之间存在明确的量化关系：Cheuvront等通过多项研究确认，当身体水分丢失达到体重的1%时，有氧耐力表现即开始出现可察觉的下降；脱水达2%体重时，计时赛成绩约下降2%-4%，核心温度升高加速，主观疲劳加剧；脱水超过3%-4%体重，将严重影响心血管功能并大幅增加热衰竭风险。更重要的是，脱水不仅通过减少血浆容量限制每搏输出量，还会减弱汗液蒸发散热能力，形成"越热越脱水、越脱水越热"的恶性循环。
赛前水合策略的目标是确保运动员以正常水合状态而非过度水合出发。赛前2-4小时内应缓慢补充5-10毫升/公斤体重的液体，并以含少量电解质的饮料为佳。例如70公斤跑者应摄取350-700毫升，避免一次性狂饮。赛前1小时可补充200-300毫升，以保持尿液呈淡黄色为简易指标。

赛中补水方案必须建立在个体化出汗率评估之上。跑者应在家中或实验室进行一次稳态出汗测试：在目标马拉松配速下跑步1小时，记录运动前后裸重、摄入液体量和尿量，计算出汗速率（升/小时 = [运动前体重(kg) - 运动后体重(kg) + 饮水量(L) - 排尿量(L)] ÷ 运动时间(h)）。例如一名跑者出汗率为1.2升/小时，赛中吸收上限通常为每小时0.6-0.8升（胃排空和肠道吸收限制），则策略应设定为每15-20分钟饮用150-200毫升运动饮料，以避免脱水积累超过体重的2%。实践中可参照场地每2.5-5公里补水站执行。
电解质补充的重点在于钠。大量出汗丢失的钠若得不到补充，将引发低钠血症，轻则头痛、恶心，重则意识模糊甚至肺水肿、脑水肿。运动饮料的理想钠含量应为500-700毫克/升（21-30毫摩尔/升），这能促进肠道对水分和糖分的共转运，同时补足部分钠丢失。

### 5. 降温方法在马拉松中的应用
科学、高效的降温干预能直接对抗核心温度的恶性攀升，延缓疲劳，保护中枢神经系统功能。方法按实施时段可分为赛前预冷、赛中降温和赛后恢复。
赛前预冷已积累丰富证据。

赛前预冷已积累丰富证据。其原理是通过降低初始体温来拓宽运动期间核心温度的上升容限。最有效的两种手段为冰浆摄入和冰背心/冷毛巾外敷。摄入冰浆（刨冰与少量液体混合，温度约-1°C）能够从内部吸收大量体热，因冰的相变潜热（融化过程吸收约334焦耳/克）远高于同质量冷水。研究表明，运动前30分钟摄入约7.5克/公斤体重的冰浆（如70公斤跑者摄入约500克），可使核心温度下降0.5-0.7°C，随后在高温运动中核心温度超过临界值的时间可推迟5-10分钟，耐力表现改善2%-5%。冰背心或预冷衣在赛前穿戴20-30分钟，通过降低皮肤温度和减少体表积热，亦有类似效果，但易受环境湿度制约。对于马拉松选手，可在热身结束、起跑等待期间使用冰背心，并结合少量分次摄入冰浆，实现内外部协同预冷。
赛中降温更依赖于赛事保障和跑者自行干预。海绵擦拭、喷淋站冷水浸润是马拉松中最常见的措施：用冷水浸湿的海绵擦拭颈部、前臂、面部，利用蒸发和传导带走热量。

### 6. 热相关疾病的识别与应对
热相关疾病构成一个连续谱，从轻度热痉挛到危及生命的热射病。马拉松跑者、配速员和赛事医护人员必须能够早期识别并果断处理。
热痉挛最常表现为下肢或腹部骨骼肌的不自主、剧烈收缩，大量出汗后仅补水而未补钠是主要诱因。处理原则为立即停止运动、转移至阴凉处，轻柔伸展痉挛肌群，并口服含钠饮料或盐水（约0.5升水中加入1克食盐），多数情况下数分钟内可缓解。若无法口服或痉挛持续，需考虑静脉输注生理盐水。热痉挛可作为警示信号，提示电解质平衡已显著偏移，若忽视可能进展为热衰竭。
热衰竭是代偿期到失代偿期的过渡状态，典型征兆为头痛、眩晕、恶心、极度疲劳、直立性头晕，以及通过大汗散热后突然停止出汗的"汗闭"现象（由体温调节中枢紊乱导致），皮肤可能转为苍白湿冷。此时核心温度常介于38.5-40°C之间。

热射病是致死性急症，特征为核心体温超过40°C并伴随中枢神经系统功能障碍，如意识模糊、行为异常、抽搐、昏迷。早期识别要点包括：皮肤干热（典型但并非绝对，部分可能湿润）、精神状态急剧变化、步态蹒跚或语无伦次。急救黄金原则是"先降温，后转运"：立即脱去衣物，将患者浸入冰水桶（2-5°C）或持续泼洒冰水并强力扇风。研究显示，冰水浸泡的降温速率可达0.15-0.35°C/分钟，而单纯表面蒸发降温约为0.08-0.10°C/分钟，一旦核心温度降至39°C以下可停止激进冷却，以防寒颤和继发性体温过低。降温启动越早，存活率和神经预后越好。切勿延误降温而等待救护车，赛事医疗团队应在现场将冰浴列为首选。

赛事保障流程应包含：赛道医疗点配备直肠温度计以准确测量核心温度，准备充盈冰水的浴池或人体冰袋，以及对工作人员进行"意识判断-体温确认-立即冰浴"的快反训练。同时，需向所有参赛者进行教育和"去耻辱化"宣导：如果感觉任何异常不适（如寒战、过度疲乏、步态不稳），主动停下来是智慧而非软弱。跑者应理解，无视预警信号而强行坚持，才是对自身和家人的不负责任。赛事手册和赛前宣讲应重复强调："倾听身体，冷却为先"的准则，使预防热射病成为马拉松安全文化的基石。
